passages.title: Who Pays for a Cup of Coffee?
passages.passage:
Few commodities travel as far, or change hands as often, as the coffee bean. By the time a cup reaches a customer in a city café, its contents have typically passed (1)____ the hands of a grower, a local collector, an exporter, a roaster and a retailer, each of (2)____ takes a share of the final price. What is striking is how unevenly that price is divided. Farmers in the highlands of East Africa or Central America commonly receive less (3)____ ten per cent of what the drinker pays, and in a poor year the figure can fall further still.

Part of the explanation lies in the structure of the market. Coffee is traded on international exchanges, (4)____ means that its price responds to weather forecasts, currency movements and speculation rather than to the cost of growing it. A frost in Brazil can double prices overnight; a bumper harvest can halve them. Growers, (5)____ contrast, cannot adjust their output quickly, because a coffee tree takes several years to bear fruit. Had they known in advance what the market would do, they might have planted differently — but nobody does.

Various schemes have been set (6)____ to address the imbalance. Certification programmes promise a guaranteed minimum price, and some roasters now buy directly from cooperatives, cutting (7)____ the middlemen altogether. Critics point out, however, that such arrangements reach only a tiny minority of the world's growers, and that the premium paid is often swallowed (8)____ by the cost of meeting the standards. It is not so (9)____ demand that is lacking as bargaining power. Until growers are able to hold stocks back when prices dip, (10)____ than sell at whatever is offered, the economics of coffee will continue to favour those furthest from the tree.

questions.explanation: Something that passes through the hands of several people is handled by each in turn. Between would need only two parties and does not collocate with hands here.
After the preposition of, a relative pronoun for people takes the object form: each of whom. Which is for things, and who cannot follow a preposition directly in formal writing.
The comparative less is completed by than: less than ten per cent. Then is a common misspelling here but is an adverb of time, not a comparative marker.

The clause comments on the whole preceding statement, so a sentential relative which means that is needed. That cannot follow a comma to refer back to a whole clause, and it would leave two main clauses joined by nothing.
By contrast (or in contrast) sets growers against the fast-moving market just described. On and for do not form a contrast linker with this noun.
To set up a scheme is to establish it. Set out means to begin a journey or to lay out a plan in detail, and set off means to depart or trigger something.
To cut out the middlemen is to remove them from the chain entirely, which altogether confirms. Cut off means to isolate or interrupt, and cut down means to reduce.

A premium that is swallowed up by costs disappears into them completely; the particle strengthens the sense of being fully absorbed. Swallowed down is about literally eating, and swallowed off does not exist.

The frame not so much X as Y corrects one explanation with a better one: what is missing is bargaining power, not demand. Not so many would need a plural countable noun, and demand is uncountable here.
Rather than sell presents holding stock back as the preferred alternative to selling cheaply. Other than means 'except', and more than would compare quantities rather than choices.

passages.title: The Race to the Ends of the Earth
passages.passage:
No sooner (1)____ the last blank spaces on the map been filled than explorers turned their attention to the poles. The attraction was not gold or trade routes, for there were none; it was the challenge of reaching a place (2)____ no human being had ever stood. Between 1890 and 1914, a succession of expeditions set out from Europe, and a good many of their members never came back.

The conditions defied preparation. Temperatures dropped so low that metal stuck to bare skin, and the wind could pin a party inside their tents for days on (3)____. Yet what proved most dangerous was often something far more ordinary: food. Expeditions carried tinned supplies, and men who lived on them for months began to suffer (4)____ scurvy, a disease whose cause was still poorly understood. Had the link with fresh food been better known, several lives would have been (5)____.

The most famous rivalry of the era was that between a Norwegian and a British party racing for the South Pole in 1911. The Norwegians, (6)____ had grown up on skis and understood dogs, arrived first and returned in good health. The British reached the Pole a month later, only to find their rivals' flag already flying, and died on the way back. Historians have argued ever (7)____ over whether the British leader was heroic or reckless. What is beyond dispute is that his diaries, recovered months afterwards, turned a failure (8)____ a legend.

Today the poles are visited by scientists and even tourists, and it is easy to forget how recently they were beyond (9)____. The men who went there had no radios and no hope of rescue. That any of them returned at (10)____ is remarkable.

questions.explanation: After No sooner at the start of a sentence, the auxiliary comes before the subject, and the earlier of the two past events takes the past perfect: No sooner had … been filled than. Were is impossible before been, and have would give the wrong time.
Place is followed by a relative adverb of location: a place where nobody had stood. Which would need a preposition (on which), and that cannot replace a place adverb.
For days on end means for many days without a break. For days on plus and or after is not a fixed expression, and on time would mean punctually.
The verb collocates with the disease as suffer from scurvy. Suffer with is a colloquial variant that examiners do not accept, and suffer of is not English.

The inverted third conditional Had … been known, lives would have been saved describes an unreal past result; spared works equally well. Lost reverses the logic, since better knowledge would not have cost lives.
A non-defining relative clause about people takes who: The Norwegians, who had grown up on skis. That is not used after a comma in a non-defining clause, and which is for things.
Ever since means continuously from that time until now, which matches the present perfect have argued. Ever after belongs to fairy tales, and ever then does not exist.
The pattern turn X into Y expresses transformation: the diaries turned a failure into a legend. Turn to means to seek help or move towards, and turn in means to hand over or go to bed.
Beyond reach means impossible to get to, which the following sentence about having no rescue confirms. Beyond belief would mean unbelievable, and beyond access is not a collocation.

At all strengthens the surprise in a clause with any: that any of them returned at all. At last would mean finally, and at least would set a minimum, neither of which fits the sense of survival against the odds.

passages.title: The Slow Death of a Language
passages.passage:
Of the roughly seven thousand languages spoken today, linguists estimate that as (1)____ as half may have vanished by the end of the century. A language does not die suddenly. It fades, generation by generation, and nearly always in the same way. First, speakers of a small language come into contact with a larger one that offers access to jobs, schooling or trade. Parents, keen for their children to get (2)____ in the wider world, begin to speak the dominant language at home. The children grow up understanding their grandparents but answering them in the new tongue. By the third generation, the old language survives only in songs, prayers and a few expressions (3)____ nobody can quite translate.

It is tempting to see this as a natural process, no more to be regretted (4)____ the extinction of a dialect of Latin. Linguists disagree, and (5)____ good reason. Every language divides up experience in its own way: some have a dozen words for kinds of snow, others mark whether a speaker witnessed an event or merely heard about it. (6)____ time such a language goes, an irreplaceable record of how human beings have made sense of their surroundings goes with it.

Efforts to reverse the decline have had mixed results. Schools that teach in a minority language can slow its loss, but they cannot on their (7)____ restore it, because a language lives in kitchens and markets, not in classrooms. Success stories exist — one Pacific island language has been brought (8)____ from a handful of elderly speakers to several thousand — but they depend on something no government can legislate: a community deciding that its language is (9)____ keeping. Without that decision, even careful documentation amounts to (10)____ more than a record of a voice already fallen silent.

questions.explanation: As many as half stresses how large the number of languages is; as much as half is also accepted because half can be read as a proportion. As far as or as long as would introduce a limit or condition, not a quantity.

To get on (or get ahead) in the world is to succeed and make progress; get by or get along, meaning to manage, are weaker but defensible. Get up or get out would lose the idea of advancement that motivates the parents.
A defining relative clause with expressions as the object of translate takes that or which. What cannot follow a noun it describes, and who is reserved for people.
No more … than makes the comparison: the loss is supposedly no sadder than the loss of a Latin dialect. As would need as much before it, and like cannot complete a more comparison.
With good reason and for good reason both mean that the disagreement is justified. In good reason and by good reason are not English expressions.

Each time or every time a language disappears, a record goes with it; the singular noun time requires a singular distributive determiner. All time is not a linker, and any time would suggest choice rather than repetition.
On their own means without help from anywhere else, which the contrast with kitchens and markets makes clear. On their part would attribute an action to them, and by their own is not idiomatic.

A language brought back from a handful of speakers has been recovered from near extinction, in the pattern bring back from the brink. Brought up means raised, and brought down means reduced or defeated.
Worth is followed directly by a gerund: worth keeping. Worthy would need of being kept, and deserving is not a natural collocation with a gerund here.
Amounts to little more than (or nothing / no more than) belittles the documentation as a mere recording. Much more than would reverse the meaning, and a little more than would need two words.

passages.title: Two Wheels and a Long Road
passages.passage:
The bicycle is (1)____ a simple machine that it is easy to assume it must always have existed. In fact, it is younger than the railway. The first recognisable ancestor appeared in Germany in 1817, when a baron built a wooden frame with two wheels (2)____ the rider pushed along with his feet. It had no pedals, no chain and no brakes, and it was ridiculed in the newspapers, (3)____ it sold in surprising numbers for a couple of summers before the novelty wore off.

Pedals were not added (4)____ the 1860s, and even then they were fixed to the front wheel, so that one turn of the legs meant one turn of the wheel. To go faster, builders simply made the front wheel bigger, (5)____ in the famous high-wheeled machine that stood taller than its rider. It was fast, elegant and dangerous: a stone in the road could send the rider flying (6)____ the handlebars, and injuries were so common that the accident had its own name, a 'header'.

The breakthrough (7)____ about in 1885 with the so-called safety bicycle. Its two wheels were the same size, its seat was low, and a chain (8)____ the pedals to the rear wheel, allowing gearing to replace sheer wheel size. Three years later an inflatable rubber tyre, invented to make a child's tricycle more comfortable, (9)____ the jolting ride into a smooth one. Within a decade, millions were cycling, women (10)____ men, and the shape settled on then has hardly changed since.

questions.explanation: Before a plus adjective plus noun, the result structure uses such … that: such a simple machine that. So would need the order so simple a machine, and too or very cannot introduce a that clause of result.

Wheels is the object of pushed, so a defining relative pronoun for things is required: wheels which the rider pushed. What cannot follow a noun, where needs a place, and whose would need a following noun.

Ridicule in the press and strong sales are in contrast, and yet joins two clauses with that meaning. So would make the sales a result of the ridicule, for would make them the reason, and nor needs a preceding negative and inversion.

Not … until marks the moment something finally happened, which even then picks up. Not added since would mean nothing has been added from that time onwards, by would leave open whether pedals were ever added, and from does not combine with a negative this way.
Only result takes the preposition in for a consequence: resulting in the high-wheeled machine. Leading would need to, and causing or producing take a direct object with no preposition.

A rider thrown forward goes over the handlebars, passing from one side to the other, which is why the accident was called a header. Above describes a position rather than a movement, across suggests a sideways path, and onto would land the rider on the bars.
Come about means to happen, so the breakthrough came about in 1885. Bring about needs an object (someone brings a change about), go about means to tackle a task, and get about means to move around.

A chain connects the pedals to the rear wheel, transmitting motion between separate parts, which is what makes gearing possible. Fixed would repeat the rigid arrangement of the earlier design, and tied or stuck describe fastening with rope or glue.

The tyre changed one thing into another, and only turn takes an object followed by into: turned the jolting ride into a smooth one. Became, got and grew describe a subject changing itself, not changing something else.
Women alongside men means both groups took part side by side. Together and along would need with, and besides men would mean 'in addition to men' in a way that does not describe shared activity.
